Pros:
1. Very low SFB especially on ring and pinky fingers
2. Far corner keys Qwerty B and Y positions are low frequency keys Q and J
3. Useful alt fingering applications with RL, HR, HL, DV, TM

Cons:
1. The SFS is quite high mostly on left index and left middle
2. Very high alternation / low roll percentage
3. Lateral stretches like RD and RM 
4. Right index PY|YP SFB

I'm on layout 14 or something at this point, and opal has been my favorite so far. (Only 108wpm so far, so these observations may change as I get back to speed).  

- Nokwts fingermap on the left hand is fantastic. Using it "normally" is comfortable, and alting anything in that triangle is intuitive.
- Similarly, I love the RHL triangle on the right hand. It introduces redirects with vowels, but being on index mitigates that. 
- I used to think that magic on the main board was a waste of space, and it's better put on a thumb, but using opal has convinced me otherwise. The repeat functionality in particular means you roll the magic key constantly, and it feels great.
- Rest of the board generally is very altable. 

I was a colstag user prior to all of this, and opal was good enough that it brought me back to rowstag (nokwts-style fingermap is not possible on colstag). 

Downside is mostly just the amount of work your right hand has. Magic mitigates things to a degree, but YI pinky can be a lot. I haven't had a huge issue with the RHL index usage, primarily because of them being tightly clustered in one region instead of a column.

Primary focus for finch is extremely low pinky usage, high rolls and not compromising on the standard stats for alternative keyboard layouts. ThEmb is used to allow for a good vowel block that has low pinky usage. Adaptive swaps are optional but do add some polish to the rough edges of the layout

Despite the limitations of pinky usage Finch comes out in the top 98th percentile for rolls, bottom 0th percentile for SFB, only 0.08% bad redirects, better than average stretch and low scissors, but with high index finger usage and not the greatest SFS though the SFS are primarily on the indexes. If you have weak pinkies, a good thumb key, stong indexes, and like rolls it's a pretty good option. 🐤️

Similarly to my more popular layout finch lyrebirds focus is very low pinky usage, high rolls and not sacrificing the other standard stats. Lyrebird improves upon finch with lower SFS, better fspeed and lower left index usage. It does this by removing the canary heritage and bringing an unusual yrts homerow that I stole from strawberryturtle (berry). Berry's strike and stray layouts are also low pinky, what lyrebird changes is optimising for column stagger, and support for 13332 keyboards such the akohekohe. To achieve this alt fingers are used for gs and sm. I have yet to type on this outside of sort tests so unproven in that regard but very interesting as it improves in basically every regard to finch.

Maybe an unpopular opinion of Gallium, it does excel in a few key aspects and it does have a notable flaw in my opinion. Gallium has an EXTREMELY good ratio of rolls in relation to its low percentage of redirects and to me this is one of its best strengths. Some other good aspects are how most of its SFBs are altable, and the SFS is pretty good too.

In terms of Gallium's main flaw I would consider RL to be too much SFB% for the ring finger to deal with since alt fingering on these positions are not ideal. This also gives Gallium an above average percentage of bad redirects due to sequences like NTR, NDR, LDN, NDL etc. Perhaps I'm too harsh but not being able to alt finger an SFB as common as RL on a weak finger is a deal breaker for me otherwise I would pick Gallium as my layout of choice (and swapping KP for better alt fingerings imo). 

Overall, I would still rank Gallium as one of the greatest layouts of all time and it's still my go to recommendation for newcomers.

custom layout that rejects home-row as resting positions for all fingers, avoids >1 key vertical travel in middle/pinky fingers, and considers alt fingerings as a resource to exploit instead of to be avoided.

achieves columnar-stagger-esque effect on standard ANSI due to its non-standard resting positions, avoids pinkies having to stretch to top-row or middles having to curl to bottom-row, and considers alts a priori instead of a posteriori on the computation of the layout's arrangement, exploiting them in order to maximize flow comfort and rolls while erasing uncomfortable scissors/redirects or SFBs/SFTs without any magic/chiral keys.

beyond the existing stats, I feel like there's many aspects that make a layout comfortable/uncomfortable that haven't yet been entirely captured. inspired by most fast typist's heavy reliance on strange alt/non-standard finger habits, i'm seeking to point them out, classify them, quantize them on an analyzer, and create a layout that's based off of these new premises, exploiting them for speed while retaining the optimal ergonomics and comfort of a properly analyzed and computed layout.

Definitely one of my favourite layouts for rowstag, and also one the best layouts that have extremely high rolls using your non-thumb fingers (though I am a thumb rolls believer), imo.

The drawbacks of this layout are of course the overloaded right index, which can cause some higher movement and sfb/sfs. This is mainly felt on a quotes corpus, but I think it will be completely fine for e200 and for every day use. I don't think its a deal breaker though because even Canary is a fine layout and that has an arguably worse left index.

I think the redirects on the right hand are fine considering they will usually involve the index, which creates a sort of anchoring effect. Also note that when you eliminate skb/sfs more than is possible with other layouts, some of this is unavoidably converted into redirects, so the raw number of redirects is maybe not as representative of the typing experience as it would be for traditional layouts.

One unique feature of the layout is that its optimised with the Mana2 scissor stat as a high priority for both regular and skip scissors. One critique of the definition is that it is overly tuned for rowstag, but in the case of Opal this is advantageous, as it creates a very nice arching and natural 'resting' position for your hands. This is most apparent if you look at the heatmap of the right hand.

A very fun layout to type on, at least for e200. Opaline, like Opal, is primarily optimised for the reddit corpus, ie every day typing, but it is particularly notable for e200 imo. There are essentially no bad words, every roll is felt, especially rolls with the thumb. This is the layout that convinced me of thumb rolls and thumb redirects being real. 

The words that distinctly don't feel flowy are words that contain thumb redirects, though I wonder if that may just be a skill issue since I've not noticed thumb reds on my right-thumb spacing sturdy which has an extreme amount of thumb redirects. One theory that I have is that after you type a word, you slow down for a little bit, and because you've slowed down a little, you don't feel the non space redirect as much. Though, I haven't seen any proof yet that you actually slow down after each word, at least for a high speed cruising e200.

The downside of this layout, like Opal, is the right index finger, although thanks to this arrangement, and the slight punctuation difference, it's far better than Opal. Though I do recommend checking out `stand-magicthemb-v2` if you want to see a version of Opaline that has more balanced index fingers, and much of the same traits, which is achieved at the slight expense of e200, but arguably is better for Reddit and quotes.

This is the best layout I've made. The reason I've made so many and swapped so frequently is I've been searching for the things that make layouts uncomfortable for me, and this has been difficult to identify. I optimize primarily for speed.

In the end, I think this sums it up:
1. High SFS/LSS indexes are uncomfortable and limit speed. Alts bringing the middle finger onto index keys being the main contributor.
2. The main stat to optimize for is SFS.
3. SFBs can be mitigated through various means, so they aren't a high priority when optimizing. <0.6% feels comfortable without being overbearing.
5. LSS is important for speed, moreso than VSS.
6. 1U scissors are uncomfortable but not a limiting factor.
7. The second stat to optimize for is 2U scissors.
8. Finger balance is important. Hand balance is too, but less so.
9. Thumb alpha is initially foreign, but is necessary for full optimization.
10. Low movement, high usage pinkies.
11. WFSpeed is useful only to guage hand balance. Ideally they are the exact same. Even better if each finger is the same. Pinkies a little less. Middles a little more.
12. Fatfingering is fine for infrequent bigrams, but too much is disruptive to flow.
13. Rolls feel nice but aren't necessary.
14. Alternation is extremely personal. Some people are limited by it, others are not.

These are what I had in mind when creating Amber. As for proof of these things, it's more of a vibe. I'm excited to learn.
